title: Time-Series Basics
html:
A time series is a sequence of observations in time order — sales per day, CPU load per minute. Order matters: neighbouring values are correlated, the future must never leak into the past, and a simple “same as last week” baseline is surprisingly hard to beat.

ComponentMeaningExample
TrendLong-term increase or decreaseGrowing user base
SeasonalityRepeating pattern with a fixed periodWeekly shopping cycle, yearly peaks
CyclesRises and falls without a fixed periodBusiness cycles
NoiseIrregular variationRandom day-to-day fluctuation

Stationarity — a series whose statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelation) don't change over time. Classical models like ARIMA assume it; trends and seasonality are removed first, e.g. by differencing (y_t − y_{t−1}, or y_t − y_{t−7} for weekly seasonality).

A forecasting example

Watch out

y.rolling(7).mean() without the shift(1) includes today's value — the very thing you are predicting. Build every lag/rolling/aggregate feature from data strictly before the prediction time, and validate with TimeSeriesSplit or a hold-out of the latest period.

Approaches

FamilyExamplesGood for
BaselinesNaive, seasonal naive, moving averageAlways — the bar to beat
Classical statisticalExponential smoothing (ETS, Holt-Winters), ARIMA/SARIMA (statsmodels)Single series, clear trend/seasonality, small data, prediction intervals
ML on engineered featuresLags, rolling stats, calendar and holiday features + gradient boosting / linear modelsMany related series, external drivers (price, promotions, weather)
Deep learningRNN/LSTM, temporal CNNs, transformers (see Deep Learning)Very many long series, complex patterns

Practical points

  • Multi-step horizons: recursive (feed predictions back as lags) accumulates errors; direct (one model per horizon) avoids that at more cost.
  • Metrics: MAE/RMSE per horizon; MASE = MAE ÷ MAE of the seasonal-naive forecast (below 1 beats the baseline); avoid MAPE with values near 0.
  • Validation: rolling-origin (expanding window) evaluation mirrors how forecasts are produced in production.
  • Label availability: if yesterday's sales are only final two days later, lag_1 isn't available at prediction time — use a gap.
  • Report prediction intervals, not only point forecasts — inventory and staffing decisions depend on the uncertainty.
How is validating a time-series model different?

The split must respect time: train on the past, validate on the following period (walk-forward / TimeSeriesSplit), never shuffle, and make sure every feature uses only information available at the forecast origin. Random K-fold leaks the future and gives optimistic errors.

What is stationarity and why does it matter?

Constant mean, variance and autocorrelation over time. ARIMA-type models assume it, and non-stationary series produce spurious correlations. Detrend or difference the series (and test with ADF/KPSS) before fitting such models; tree models on lag features are more forgiving but still can't extrapolate a trend.

What baseline would you use for a forecasting problem?

The naive forecast (last value) and the seasonal naive forecast (value one season ago, e.g. same weekday last week). Many sophisticated models fail to beat them; MASE expresses error relative to that baseline.
